item.title: Thursday, October 22, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk. One: PulteGroup reports third-quarter results this morning, and the incentive and rate-buydown spend is the best read we get on how much pain is in new construction. Two: Freddie Mac's weekly survey publishes today and the daily tracker went into it flat at 7.40 percent, so this is a plateau rather than a rally — with the FOMC minutes pointing to another increase and the 10-year at 5.13 percent, the case for locking rather than floating is about as strong as it gets. Three: pending sales fell 7.3 percent and months of supply is up to 4.8, so November and December closings are already thinner than September's — rebuild the pipeline this week and price listings to the slower market. And three things for the world. One: the Strait of Hormuz remains shut on Iran's terms, with oil flows at roughly 68 percent of pre-war levels and Brent touching 111.99 dollars, and nothing is expected to move before the US midterms on 3 November. Two: Meta posted a record 64.6 billion dollars of quarterly revenue and committed up to 145 billion dollars to AI infrastructure while absorbing a 10 billion dollar settlement charge. Three: Barcelona host Real Madrid on Sunday with six points between them at the top of La Liga.

item.title: Tuesday, October 20, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk. First, today: September housing starts and permits at 8:30am Eastern and September pending home sales at 10am — pending sales is the freshest read on September contracts because existing home sales do not print again until 12 November. Second, 43 percent of builders cut prices in October averaging 6 percent, with 65 percent stacking incentives — pull new-development incentive sheets into your resale negotiations this week, because your sellers are competing with a 6 percent discount whether they know it or not. Third, the FOMC meets 28 October with the funds range at 3.75 to 4.00 percent and the market seriously debating a hike rather than a cut — stop telling buyers to wait for spring, and anyone with a lock expiring in three weeks should be having that conversation today. And three things for the world. One, President Trump suspended a tranche of Russia sanctions two days before they would have taken effect, drawing bipartisan criticism, while Putin has floated a three-way summit with Trump and Xi next month. Two, France saw protests across more than 140 cities turn violent with more than 2,000 detained, and Macron has refused his interior minister's offered resignation. Three, Israel votes on 27 October, its first election since October 2023, with most polling showing Netanyahu's coalition short of a majority.

item.title: Sunday, October 18, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk. The daily thirty-year fixed is down twenty-seven basis points since October seventh to 7.37 percent, while Freddie Mac still prints 7.40 percent unchanged, so quote the daily number this week and tell anyone waiting on the Fed that the October twenty-eighth debate is hold-versus-hike, not a cut. New Jersey inventory rose again in September, so buyer leverage is returning in the mid tiers and anything sitting more than three weeks needs a pricing revisit. Housing starts and permits land Tuesday, and the FHFA sets the 2027 conforming loan limits in about five weeks, so clients hovering just above 832,750 dollars may land back inside conforming by waiting. Also in this episode: hot September inflation met by falling yields on AI-debt fears, the Graham Act sanctions waiver on Russia, Saturday's No Kings early-voting day of action, a 4.5 percent weekly fall in the Nasdaq against a 0.7 percent gain for the Dow, the New Jersey pharma headquarters layoffs, and Real Madrid's four-three comeback in Rome.

item.title: Saturday, October 17, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk. One: the late-October Fed meeting now carries a 17 percent hike probability and December stands at 89 percent, so lock or close anything rate-sensitive before that meeting. Two: stop selling rate cuts and start selling spread, because the gap between the 10-year Treasury and the 30-year mortgage is roughly 230 basis points against a long-run normal nearer 170, and that 60-point cushion is where realistic relief comes from. Three: office tenant leverage is closing, with sublease space at a six-year low and new completions heading for a 30-year low, so open any renewal inside 18 months now rather than next spring. And three things for the world. One: Alberta votes Monday on whether to begin leaving Canada. Two: Brazil's presidential runoff is on 25 October, with the courts putting Meta's algorithm formally on notice. Three: the Nasdaq has just had its worst week since June, down 4.5 percent, as the argument shifts from whether AI is transformative to whether it is overpriced.

item.title: Thursday, October 15, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk. First, and it is tomorrow: the NAHB builder sentiment index for October lands Friday the sixteenth; September was 32, a three-year low, and a lower print means builder incentives rather than price cuts and a thinner 2027 supply pipeline. Second, the FOMC meets October 27th and 28th and after Wednesday's hot September CPI the risk is a hike, not a cut, so strip rate-fall assumptions out of every pipeline file and have the lock conversation today. Third, national inventory is up 4.6% year on year with 4.8 months of supply and 33 days on market, which is buyer leverage, but the Northeast median is up 4.7% year on year, the strongest gain in the country, so price to the region and ask for concessions rather than price cuts on the buy side. And three things for the world. Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer and has had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in successful surgery. India has removed roughly 130 million names from its electoral rolls, triggering the largest challenge to its Election Commission in years. And the Houthis struck Saudi Aramco's own headquarters in Dhahran, with Brent around 108 dollars a barrel. Also in this episode: 30-year mortgage at 7.45%, Freddie Mac at 7.40%, the 10-year Treasury just under 5.2%, FHFA easing credit-data rules, Netflix cutting 1,000 jobs, Real Madrid winning 4-3 at Roma, and the Upper West Side going on a fast track for affordable housing.

item.title: Wednesday, October 14, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk: the weekly thirty-year fixed is at 7.40 percent, the highest in about three years, up from 7.28 percent the week before, and the next weekly print lands Thursday 15 October, so have your talking points ready today and lead with the payment rather than the rate. The final phase of the Portal North Bridge cutover has NJ Transit running reduced service for roughly five weeks through about 15 November, with the Montclair-Boonton Line specifically affected, so sellers on those lines should discuss timing today and buyers testing commutes this month are sampling the worst version of it. And stop selling the rate cut: there is no Fed meeting this week, the next falls at the end of October, and Treasury yields set fresh highs at the start of this week, so price the deal on today's payment. Also in this episode: Washington weighs joining a Saudi-led offensive in Yemen while Iran's Revolutionary Guard strikes three ships in two days near the Strait of Hormuz; at least 139 people including 15 children die when a migrant boat from Djibouti to Yemen capsizes; the Supreme Court takes up whether DOGE is subject to FOIA; Goldman Sachs beats big and JPMorgan posts a rare miss as bank earnings season opens; the weekend box office and a notable flop; and Real Madrid beat Villarreal 1-0 ahead of Sunday's Sevilla fixture and the Clasico on 25 October. A shorter brief than usual, with unverifiable figures dropped rather than guessed.

item.title: Sunday, October 11, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk: NJ Transit and Amtrak begin five weeks of Northeast Corridor disruption today for the Portal North Bridge second-track tie-in, so warn every commuter client and rethink any showing that assumes a clean train ride. Wednesday brings the September CPI print and lenders are holding a 220 basis point spread over the 10-year specifically because they are waiting for it, so a float held to Wednesday afternoon is a real option worth pricing; watch Monday too, when FHFA Director Bill Pulte may announce the two-bureau credit report change at the MBA convention. And the refinance channel is down 56 percent year on year with the 30-year at 7.40 percent on the Freddie Mac survey and 7.48 percent on the daily tracker, so the conversation is buydowns, adjustable-rate products and the FHA option pricing 35 basis points inside conforming. Also in today's brief: a strike on Riyadh's main airport killed at least 12 and wounded 309, with President Trump saying he may take the US into the Yemen war; diesel at 6.28 dollars a gallon against 3.68 a year ago; Manhattan office vacancy at 12.6 percent, the lowest since before 2020; the S&P 500 up 1.2 percent on the week; SpaceX buying 8 billion dollars of spectrum and taking T-Mobile down 13 percent; and Real Madrid beating Villarreal 1-0 with Vinicius sent off.

item.title: Saturday, October 10, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk: the Portal North Bridge cutover starts Sunday 11 October and runs five weeks through 14 November, cutting weekday Midtown Direct service and terminating Morris & Essex, Gladstone and Montclair-Boonton trains at Hoboken, so move weekday Manhattan showings and closings earlier or route clients via PATH and tell Morris & Essex clients today; stop quoting summer mortgage rates, because Freddie Mac now prints 7.40 percent after seven straight weekly increases and the September FOMC minutes point to another hike rather than a cut, so re-run every pre-approval older than a month; and put 28 October in the diary, as that Fed decision is being previewed as hike-or-hold with the 10-year Treasury near a 24-year high, so extend any rate lock expiring near that date now. And three things for the world: Navi Pillay, the South African jurist now sitting on the International Court of Justice, won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize; SpaceX is paying about 8 billion dollars for nationwide 800 MHz low-band spectrum, knocking more than 9 percent off T-Mobile in a single session; and the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is now the deadliest on record, past 4,100 deaths, with Kenya recording its first imported case.

item.title: Friday, October 9, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk: the FOMC meets 27-28 October and the September minutes point to hikes rather than cuts, so execute rate locks before that meeting instead of floating into it; rates are about 110 basis points above a year ago, roughly 290 dollars a month more on a 400,000 dollar loan, so rebuild client conversations around monthly payment and buy-downs and have every shopper collect multiple quotes; and 65 billion dollars of commercial real estate debt matures this year into spreading distress beyond office, so pull the next two quarters of maturities today and start those refinance conversations. And three things for the world: Navi Pillay, the former UN human rights chief, won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize; Congress averted a shutdown with federal funding now running to 11 December; and the 10-year Treasury yield is pressing a 24-year high, putting the cost of long money at its highest in roughly a generation.

item.title: Thursday, October 8, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk: One, stop quoting the weekly survey — the daily trackers have the thirty-year at or above 7.5% while Freddie Mac still says 7.28%, and a new Freddie Mac print lands at noon today; re-qualify every pre-approval written in August, because 60 basis points has moved the goalposts. Two, ask your lenders whether they are pricing the FHFA's bi-merge change, two credit reports instead of three — a real cost saving at application and a better read for thin-file buyers. Three, work the Jersey City versus Manhattan rent divergence alongside the New Jersey layoff file: Jersey City rents are falling because supply arrived, Manhattan's are at records because nobody can move, and September's notices in Princeton, Plainsboro and Hudson County will surface as relocation listings in roughly ninety days. Also in this episode: the 10-year Treasury at a 24-year high, divided FOMC minutes after September's hike to 3.75-4%, Hurricane Isaias bearing down on the Gulf Coast, the Hormuz tanker strike, Spain's housing decree, record-then-retreat equity markets, Verity's $32.6m box office win, the $111bn Skydance-Warner Bros Discovery close, and Real Madrid team news ahead of Villarreal.

item.title: Sunday, October 4, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk. One, the G train signal works begin Monday 5 October and run through 26 October, so Brooklyn showings on that corridor need rerouting now. Two, the New York City rent freeze is live as of 1 October, with stabilised renewals at zero percent on both one- and two-year leases through next September, so stabilised assets need re-underwriting and renewal notices need checking against the new order. Three, stop waiting for the Fed: its last move was a hike, a cut on 28 October is priced at roughly two percent, and Freddie Mac's weekly survey at 7.28 percent is already lagging a daily market at 7.57 percent, so lock what you can lock now. And three things for the world. One, Brazil votes today in the first round of its general election, with a runoff on 25 October if nobody clears fifty percent, Lula against Flavio Bolsonaro. Two, the United Arab Emirates has formally ruled the Flydubai cockpit attack an attempted terrorist act, with 174 people aboard the Dubai to Tel Aviv flight. Three, Tom Cruise's Digger opened at 7.5 million dollars against a budget of up to 160 million, one of the year's most expensive box office failures.

item.title: Thursday, October 1, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk. One: the ninth of October is the deadline — Portal North Bridge work cuts New York Penn Station service from 10 October through 15 November, and every weekday Midtown Direct train is rerouted to Hoboken, so move Manhattan showings and closings off those trains and warn commuting buyers now. Two: a new Freddie Mac survey prints today around midday; the last read 7.03 percent, and the gap to 6.30 percent a year ago is 242 dollars a month on a 500,000 dollar loan, so reprice affordability sheets the moment it lands. Three: Governor Sherrill's housing plan names Red Bank, Bayonne and Linden for transit-oriented development, doubles state-land production to 40,000 units and puts a shot clock on permits — set alerts on those towns and ask developer clients what a mandated approval timeline does to their option periods. And three things for the world. One: the Supreme Court has allowed deportations to third countries to resume while it weighs the policy, over the dissent of three justices. Two: the Federal Reserve raised rates unanimously on 16 September to a target range of 3.75 to 4 percent and said inflation remains elevated — the direction of travel is up, not down. Three: Brent crude is above 100 dollars a barrel, nearly 36 dollars higher than a year ago, the cleanest explanation of why the inflation fight is not finished.

item.title: Monday, September 28, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk: Quote the daily rate, not the weekly one — Mortgage News Daily had the 30-year fixed at 7.43% on Sept 25 against Freddie Mac's 7.03% weekly survey, a 40 basis point gap, and the daily figure is what your buyer's lock will reflect. The NAR commission settlement claims deadline is reportedly October 27 — verify it on the official litigation site this week and notify any client who transacted in the covered window. And split your pipeline by price band: KBW's downgrade of Lennar and upgrade of Toll Brothers says the entry-level buyer is the one who walks, so the bottom band needs a rate conversation and the top band does not. Also in this episode: the 10-year Treasury at 5.17% and a near-normal 186 basis point mortgage spread, meaning relief has to come from the bond market rather than from lenders; the Fed's September 16 hike to 3.75-4.00% with more signalled; the US-China $30 billion tariff product lists; the nor'easter that killed one and cut power to more than 130,000 across the Northeast; New Jersey Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell's resignation over an ethics and harassment report; a crowded box office led by an Avengers Endgame re-release at $26 million; and Real Madrid sitting second in La Liga on 15 points after the derby defeat at Atletico.

item.title: Thursday, September 24, 2026
item.description: Three things for the desk. One: the daily thirty-year fixed is 7.26 percent, its highest since May 2024, and the ten-year Treasury hit 5.10 percent on Wednesday, a nineteen-year high, after moving nine basis points in a single session, so anyone floating a rate should be having the lock conversation today rather than next week. Two: Freddie Mac's weekly survey says 6.95 percent while the lock desk quotes 7.26 percent, and that gap needs explaining to every client before they find it themselves at the closing table. Three: Case-Shiller lands Tuesday the 29th and existing home sales have now fallen three months running to a 3.98 million annual pace, so have the line ready on why volume is falling faster than price, which is lock-in rather than a demand collapse. Also in this episode: the Fed's unanimous 25 basis point hike to 3.75 to 4.00 percent and a dot plot showing no return to 2 percent inflation until 2029, a wave of Manhattan office towers back on the sale market, the UN General Assembly high-level week, Lavrov ruling out a ceasefire, Wednesday's selloff across all four major indexes, Holtec pulling its IPO and Bristol Myers Squibb cutting 265 New Jersey jobs, a 60 million dollar opening for Resident Evil, and Valverde out roughly three weeks for Real Madrid.
